title: Lookups across a row
summary: Look up months across a row of headings and return the matching sales and target from rows below.

blocks.text: The monthly sales summary for an Eldoret store is laid out across the page: months run along row 1, with sales in row 2 and target in row 3. A manager wants to pick any month and see the sales, the target, the variance and a status.
Because the months are in a row, the lookup range is a row too. XLOOKUP works the same way, but the return range must also be a row of the same length.

items: Objective: use XLOOKUP on a row-oriented list and keep the lookup and return ranges the same shape.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: The months are in B1:G1, which is a row of 6 cells. The return range B2:G2 is also a row of 6 cells, so they line up. XLOOKUP finds May in the 5th cell and returns the 5th cell of the sales row.

blocks.caption: Monthly summary in A1:G3 (K = KES thousands)

blocks.text: Looking up May in the sales row gives 5,100K. Looking it up with the target row as the return range, $B$3:$G$3, gives 5,000K.
B$5 holds the month to find. The $ before the 5 keeps the row fixed, while the column letter changes when you copy the formula across to C and D. This is called a mixed reference.

items: A row lookup needs a row return range: $B$1:$G$1 with $B$2:$G$2 works.
A row of 6 cells with a column of 6 cells does not work. For example $B$1:$G$1 with $A$2:$A$7 gives #VALUE!, because the shapes differ even though the counts are equal.
Months and sizes are often laid out as headings across the top. XLOOKUP reads them in either direction without any change to the formula pattern.

blocks.text: Tip: when you copy a formula across, ask which references should stay and which should move. Put $ in front of what must stay.
Use the monthly summary from Training (A1:G3). Type numbers without commas. A negative number needs a minus sign.

items: XLOOKUP works across a row exactly as it does down a column.
The lookup range and the return range must both be rows of the same length.
A row with a column of the same count still gives #VALUE!.
Use a mixed reference such as B$5 to copy a formula across.

blocks.text: A row layout needs no new function, only matching row-shaped ranges.

items.prompt: What does =XLOOKUP("Mar",$B$1:$G$1,$A$2:$A$7) show, where $A$2:$A$7 is a column of 6 cells?

options.label: #VALUE!, because a row lookup range needs a row return range
The value for March from column A
#N/A, because Mar is not in the list

items.prompt: Variance is sales minus target. What is the variance for April, in K? Use a minus sign if it is negative.
Why is the month written as B$5 in the formula in B6, then copied across to C6 and D6?

options.label: The $ keeps the row at 5, while the column moves to C5 and D5
The $ keeps the column at B
